transcript:
[00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're Samira from Redwood, with Diego from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Jordan Lee: Good, yeah thanks. Sorry we had to squeeze this in, schedule was tight.
[00:10] Maya Singh: Hey all. We're excited, we did some light reading on Redwood plus watched the dedicated overview.
[00:18] Samira Patel: Great — quick agenda: we want to understand your current stack, migration goals from OpenAI, any constraints (security, latency, cost), and propose next steps.
[00:26] Elliot Park: Sounds good. Quick context: LynxAI is a search/assistant startup, heavy retrieval augmented generation. We currently call OpenAI APIs (gpt-4o-ish and embeddings), and have some in-house running vLLM for private models. Our main ask: reduce token costs and get more control/observability while keeping eval parity.
[00:44] Diego Morales: Nice, thanks. When you say "eval parity", do you mean response quality on your test prompts, latency SLO, or both?
[00:50] Jordan Lee: Both. We have a 2k prompt eval set and for our internal metrics response quality drop cannot be more than ~2% vs OpenAI. Latency ideally at or under current 450ms median for short prompts.
[01:05] Maya Singh: Also we need strict audit logs for compliance and KMS integration for keying.
[01:11] Samira Patel: Totally. On the Dedicated side, we run isolated GPU pools, customer-dedicated models, and you can integrate KMS/HSM + VPC peering. We are SOC 2 and have an enterprise security pack. I'll send the security deck after this — link in notes.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: Cool. One question: we're using vLLM and TGI in some experiments. How compatible is Redwood with those runtimes?
[01:34] Diego Morales: Short answer — we support models that run on PyTorch/TorchServe and many of the HF formats. We also support running your own vLLM-backed instances as a custom runtime in Private deployments, but for Hosted/Dedicated we typically onboard the model into Redwood's runtime where we handle KV cache, batching, and optimized kernels. There can be small differences in tokenizer handling and sampling defaults so we recommend an eval pass.
[01:53] Maya Singh: When you say "small differences" can you give an example?
[01:57] Diego Morales: Sure — for instance, some TGI setups default to top-p configs, or use different temperature scheduling; and tokenization of special tokens can vary slightly which affects logprobs. We surface sampling params and you can pin them to ensure parity.
[02:11] Jordan Lee: Ok. For our internal models we sometimes rely on certain KV cache behavior in vLLM per request. Will that impact latency?
[02:19] Diego Morales: Our runtime exposes KV cache semantics and supports continuous batching with preserved KV for sessions. For RLHF-type sessions you'd see similar latency; ops differ depending on sequence length. For short prompts your median should be comparable, though exact numbers depend on GPU and batch config.
[02:36] Samira Patel: Also worth noting we do model variants: we can run the same model quantized for cost savings with shown perf regressions and you can A/B test.
[02:45] Avery (PM): How does fallbacks work? Say capacity is constrained.
[02:48] Samira Patel: We support automatic fallback to compatible model variants or routed regions; for Dedicated contract customers we set reserved capacity and burst options to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[02:57] Elliot Park: Security: we need KMS for key rotation and retention policies, plus audit trails for all requests. How are logs stored and who has access?
[03:05] Diego Morales: Logs can be retained in your account or shipped to your SIEM; audit logs include token-level metadata but we can redact PII. Access is RBAC-controlled and integrated with SSO/SAML. We'll share the security pack that details retention, encryption-at-rest, and KMS support.
[03:24] Jordan Lee: Great, please send that.
[03:27] Samira Patel: Will do. Now, timeline: what's your target migration window?
[03:31] Jordan Lee: We want a pilot in April and production by Q3 if the pilot is successful. Our procurement cycle is light but security review is heavy.
[03:40] Maya Singh: Also a note — some of our prompts are long, up to 8k tokens with retrieval context. How does Redwood handle long contexts?
[03:48] Diego Morales: We support models with up to X tokens depending on the model size and have optimized attention kernels; beyond a threshold we recommend prefix caching and segmented retrieval to keep perf predictable. For 8k we typically run a mid-size A100 or H100 with tuned kernels. We'll detail hardware suggestions in the benchmark sheet.
[04:06] Jordan Lee: Is there an easy way to run our eval set against Redwood to check parity?
[04:10] Diego Morales: Yes — we provide a benchmark template (Google Sheet) and a small runner (docker image) that will call a demo endpoint or your Dedicated instance. You can run locally with a Redwood endpoint key or we can run it on our side with a masked dataset. We'll share the instructions.
[04:25] Maya Singh: We want to avoid sending raw PII to third parties, so if you run it we'd need a scrubbed set.
[04:31] Samira Patel: Totally understood. Either share a scrubbed eval or we'll run with your masked data under the pilot NDA.
[04:38] Jordan Lee: Cost — can you ballpark savings vs OpenAI? We're at about $70k/month right now on tokens.
[04:45] Samira Patel: Ballpark for Dedicated depends on model and usage pattern, but many customers see 30–60% unit cost reduction with batching, prefix caching, and quantized variants. We'll build a cost model for you given your token distribution.
[04:58] Jordan Lee: Nice. Do you support hybrid routes — some traffic to hosted, some to Dedicated?
[05:03] Diego Morales: Yes, routing by policy is supported — you can set latency-first routes and cheaper-model routes by traffic type.
[05:09] Avery (PM): Procurement: what does a Dedicated contract look like — term lengths, commitments?
[05:14] Samira Patel: Typically 12–36 month reserved capacity with monthly commit; we can structure burst credits and flexible scaling. We'll include term options in the pricing doc.
[05:23] Jordan Lee: Regarding model licensing — we also use some community-licensed models. Any IP issues?
[05:27] Diego Morales: We onboard models per licensing terms and will surface any restrictions. For private deployments we can bring-your-own-model. For hosted/dedicated we maintain compliance checks.
[05:36] Maya Singh: One last technical thing — we rely on custom CUDA kernels in some vLLM configs. Will Redwood lose that optimization?
[05:43] Diego Morales: Redwood chooses kernels per architecture; if you have custom kernels in vLLM that are proprietary, Private deployment (customer-managed) is the safest for preserving them. For Dedicated, we can often match behavior via our kernel selection but we'd need to benchmark.
[05:59] Jordan Lee: Good to know.
[06:02] Samira Patel: Ok let's recap next steps: we'll send pricing + security pack, Diego will send migration checklist and benchmark runner, and we'll schedule a technical deep dive focused on infra and kernels.
[06:13] Elliot Park: Can we get a proposed date for the technical deep dive?
[06:16] Diego Morales: I can do week of 2026-03-09 — how's Tuesday or Thursday for you?
[06:21] Jordan Lee: Thursday works.
[06:23] Avery (PM): Good. Also we need to confirm data residency — some customers in EU require regional hosting. We need EMEA availability.
[06:31] Samira Patel: We have EU regions available for Dedicated and Private; we'll include region pricing.
[06:36] Maya Singh: Alright. Anything else?
[06:38] Jordan Lee: One more item — can you share any benchmark examples where you migrated from OpenAI and saw parity?
[06:44] Samira Patel: Yes, we have a benchmark deck and a few case studies; I'll attach them.
[06:48] Jordan Lee: Perfect.
[06:50] [crosstalk]
[06:53] Samira Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and set the tech deep dive.
[06:57] Jordan Lee: Thanks, appreciate it.
[07:00] Maya Singh: Thanks.
[07:02] Diego Morales: Bye all.
